In physics, a '''fundamental''' particle<ref>{{#cite:Q1942}}</ref>

* has no substructure
** i.e., is not made of other particles
* has no finite size other than its wavelength $\lambda$

== History ==

[[File:Are you a fundamental particle.png|thumbnail]]

In the 19th century, scientists believed [[atom]]s to be fundamental particles.<ref>{{#cite:Q1793}}</ref> The name atom, from Greek ''ἄτομος'', literally means 'indivisible'. It was not until the beginning This belief was idely-held until [[quark]]s, whose existence was first hypothesised in the 1960s, were experimentally discovered in the 1970s.<ref>{{#cite:Q1942}}</ref>

== Types ==

According to the [[standard model of particle physics]], there are three types of fundamental particles: '''[[Lepton]]s''' and '''[[quark]]s''', which form '''[[matter]]''', and '''[[boson]]s''', which are carrier particles of the four [[fundamental forces]] through which the leptons and quarks interact with each other.

Each fundamental particle also has a corresponding [[antiparticle]], forming [[antimatter]] and facilitating their interactions.

Each of the three types of fundamental particles can be further divided into roughly three families, of which the first is normal matter, containing stable particles.

[[File:Fundamental particles.jpeg|500px|center]]

Quarks and leptons in family 2 and 3 are observed to decay into stable particles in family 1. The relationship between the different bosons is an area of active research.<ref>{{#cite:Q1942}}</ref>

Various known fundamental particles are listed below:

[[File:Fundamental-particles.jpg|500px|center]]

<blockquote>
Quarks and leptons are together known as '''fermions''', whereas bosons are also known as '''carrier particles'''.
